claims.text: Penalizing differences between distributions of predictions across demographic groups induces nearly-universal degradation of within-group performance metrics.
Penalizing group fairness violations results in heterogeneous effects on measures of fairness in calibration and cross-group ranking across experimental conditions.
Penalizing demographic parity violations increases the AUROC of the 30-day readmission model for the Black population at lambda = 3.6 from 0.66 to 0.69 compared to baseline.
Penalizing demographic parity violations increases the average precision of the 30-day readmission model for the Black population at lambda = 3.6 from 0.15 to 0.17 compared to baseline.

Applying conditional penalties in the outcome-positive strata to encourage equal opportunity for 30-day readmission prediction in STARR by sex increases equal opportunity violation at lambda = 10 (MEqOpp = 0.0069) relative to baseline (MEqOpp = 0.0056).
Unconstrained baseline clinical risk prediction models exhibit substantial variations in group-level performance metrics, conditional prediction parity, and cross-group ranking accuracy.

evidence.description: With few exceptions, the effect of increasing the weight on conditional regularization penalties targeting equalized odds or equal opportunity is a monotonic reduction in group-level model performance measures for all groups across datasets.

Both unconditional and conditional penalties can introduce relative calibration error across groups in a manner unrelated to absolute calibration changes, concentrating in relatively few demographic groups.

Penalizing the violation of demographic parity increases the performance of the model that predicts 30-day readmission for the Black population when lambda = 3.6 compared to baseline (AUROC: 0.69 vs. 0.66).
Average precision for the Black population in the 30-day readmission model increased to 0.17 at lambda = 3.6 compared to 0.15 at baseline.

When using a conditional penalty in the outcome-positive strata for 30-day readmission in STARR by sex, equal opportunity violation was greater at lambda = 10 (MEqOpp = 0.0069) than at baseline (MEqOpp = 0.0056).
In the unpenalized 30-day readmission model in STARR, baseline AUROC across race/ethnicity groups varied from 0.66 for the Black population to 0.80 for the Other population group.

methodologies.name: Fairness-regularized feedforward neural network risk prediction benchmark
methodologies.description: Fully-connected feedforward neural networks trained with six regularization strategies penalizing demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity violations across log-spaced regularization weights lambda.

limitations.text: Metrics and regularizers were constructed using one-versus-marginal comparisons, which inherently make metrics for over-represented groups smaller because those groups comprise a larger fraction of the aggregate population.
The use of soft penalized learning objectives rather than constrained optimization formulations may exaggerate the severity of performance-fairness trade-offs.

The group fairness framework treats sensitive attributes as abstract discrete categories, reinforcing demographic taxonomies while failing to capture intersectional identities or causal mechanisms of structural racism.

Typical algorithmic fairness formulations are unaware of systemic context and measurement error in retrospective data, making criteria misleading when observed outcomes are biased surrogates for constructs of interest.

future_work.text: Evaluate whether constrained non-convex optimization reformulations (such as proxy-Lagrangian formulations) satisfy group fairness criteria with fewer performance trade-offs than soft penalties.
Incorporate participatory design practices with diverse stakeholders and decision-theoretic causal frameworks to evaluate algorithmic interventions within broader sociotechnical contexts.
